source.title: Evaluating Evaluation Metrics - The Mirage of Hallucination Detection
source.authors: Atharva Kulkarni; Yuan Zhang; Joel Ruben Antony Moniz; Xiou Ge; Bo-Hsiang Tseng; Dhivya Piraviperumal; S. Swayamdipta; Hong Yu

record.tranche_reason: The study varies language-model size and reports that hallucination metrics generally lack consistent or monotonic gains, challenging predictable downstream scaling in this tested setting.
record.gate_note: The study does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy, fit power laws, or test compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. It tests hallucination metrics on generated outputs as language-model size varies. Other cited scaling-law findings are background, not results of this study.
record.test_reason: It compares downstream hallucination/factuality scores on TruthfulQA and FaithDial across 37 models (125M–70B), with significance tests for a size effect. That bears on V6 in a new setting. It is uncontrolled scaling: sizes mix five families plus pretrained and instruction-tuned models, and no curve or loss relation is fitted. The authors read the lack of gains as a flaw in the metrics, not a failure of scaling, so T3 fits better than T5.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that most hallucination metrics do not improve steadily with model size and that only the GPT-4 judge consistently does. They read this as a sign that the metrics are poorly designed or misaligned with the task, not as evidence against scaling.
record.recipe_differences: Rather than fitting held-out pretraining-loss curves or optimizing parameter/token allocations, the study compares hallucination metric outcomes on generations from models of different sizes.
record.method_sensitivity: Metric and dataset change the reported scaling pattern; Gemma abstention also produces divergent metric readings.
record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, 2025
record.problems: The size-scaling evidence is limited to hallucination metrics on TruthfulQA and FaithDial, not held-out pretraining loss or broad downstream capability. The main size trends are presented in figures without raw values in the text; the paper also gives potentially inconsistent descriptions of some significance results and metric trends.
record.rows_left_out: Individual model/checkpoint values and additional metric curves in Figures 3, 13, 14, and 15 were not transcribed; the text does not give their numeric values. The retained rows include the size-effect p-values from Table 2 and the paper's explicit qualitative descriptions.

untested.parts: Performance as a function of pretraining loss. Any fitted functional form or prediction of larger models. Controlled within-family scaling separated from instruction tuning. Downstream tasks beyond knowledge-grounded dialog and factual QA.

missing.what: Q2 token-F1, MSP and perplexity improve with model size; other NLG, overlap and uncertainty metrics show no consistent pattern.

record.verdict_notes: The record's Table 2 values are partly misread. The columns run TQA training, TQA size, TQA decoding, FD training, FD size, FD decoding. This is confirmed by the text's claim that Sacrebleu (0.246) and K-BertScore (0.116) are non-significant for instruction tuning on FaithDial. Size bins pool different families and pretrained and instruction-tuned models, so the size effect is confounded. The GPT-4 judge is actually gpt-4o-mini.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining cross-entropy scaling with parameter count, tokens, or compute.
No small-run power-law fits or predictions of substantially larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or parameter/token allocation law.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.
No tests of power-law form in other modalities or training regimes.
Tests only hallucination-related metric outcomes on TruthfulQA and FaithDial as model size varies; it does not test downstream tasks broadly or performance as a function of pretraining loss.
No comparison of scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal allocations across fitting choices, parameter-counting conventions, or training setups.

rows.subject: Gemma 1 and Gemma 1.1 models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared hallucination metric outputs across Gemma model sizes and versions.
rows.value: Gemma 1 and 1.1 results often suggest opposite conclusions; the authors attribute this to Gemma models abstaining from answers.
rows.note: The authors say abstention explains low K-BertScore but higher Critic and GPT-4 scores.
rows.check: This is a metric-disagreement observation (Gemma abstention), not a size trend. It should not be linked to V6.

relationships.condition: GPT-4(o-mini) judge and Rouge-L, on TruthfulQA and FaithDial, greedy decoding
relationships.reason: Authors say the GPT-4 judge improves with size (p=0.0 on both datasets, R9, R18). Appendix C.4 says Rouge-L improves with size (R1, R10).
relationships.display_finding: The authors reported improving GPT-4 judge scores with size, with p=0.0 on both datasets, alongside improving Rouge-L scores.

relationships.condition: Other hallucination metrics (BertScore, K-BertScore, Consistency, Q2 NLI, Critic)
relationships.reason: Gains with size depend on the metric. Effects are non-significant (R3, R6, R14, R17), small (R16), contradictory across datasets (R21) or deteriorating (R20), with no monotonic pattern overall (R19). The authors attribute this to metric misalignment with the task.
relationships.display_finding: Size effects were small, nonsignificant, inconsistent across datasets, or negative, with no overall monotonic pattern; the authors attributed this to metric misalignment.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Hallucination metrics other than GPT-4 across TruthfulQA and FaithDial
reader_labels.reason: The authors report no clear monotonic pattern overall, deterioration for K-BertScore on TruthfulQA, and inconsistent or absent size effects for several metrics (R2-R8, R10-R17, R19-R21).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: GPT-4 hallucination metric on TruthfulQA and FaithDial
reader_labels.reason: The authors report that GPT-4 performance improves with model size on both datasets and give p = 0.0 for each size-effect test (R9, R18).

reader_labels.reason: Gemma 1 and 1.1 can yield opposite conclusions across metrics, with abstention cited as an explanation (R22).
